  LAND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
  We would like to acknowledge that the land we inhabit today was once known as
  Tovangaar, the home of the Gabrieleño-Tongva people. We show our respect to the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, as well as all Indigenous people, past, present, and future,
  and honor their labor as original caretakers of this land. We commit to uplifting the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, invite you to acknowledge the history, and join us in caring
  for this land.

GENERAL INFORMATION
Documents related to an Agenda item are available to the public in the City Clerk’s Office located at 320
West Newmark Avenue, Monterey Park, CA 91754, during normal business hours and the City’s website
at www.montereypark.ca.gov/AgendaCenter/City-Council-17.

The public may watch the meeting live on the city’s cable channel MPKTV (AT&T U-verse, channel 99
or Charter Communications, channel 182) or by visiting the city’s website at
www.montereypark.ca.gov/133/City-Council-Meeting-Videos. Per the Americans with Disabilities Act, if
you need special assistance to participate in this meeting, please call City Hall at (626) 307-1359 for
reasonable accommodation at least 24 hours before a meeting. Council Chambers are wheelchair
accessible.

PUBLIC PARTICIPATION
You may speak up to 5 minutes on an/each Agenda item. You may combine up to 2 minutes of time with
another person’s speaking. No person may speak more than a total of 10 minutes. The Mayor and City
Council may change the amount of time allowed for speakers. Written Communication will be accepted
up  to  24  hours  before  the  meeting  by  completing  an  online  form  at
www.montereypark.ca.gov/writtencomm.

item not on the agenda. The Council may briefly respond to comments after Public Communications is
closed. Persons may, in addition to any other matter within the City Council's subject-matter jurisdiction,
comment on Agenda Items at this time. If you provide public comment on a specific Agenda item at this

2-B.  DISCUSSION OF FINDINGS ON CITY’S UPDATED INCLUSIONARY HOUSING
  ORDINANCE FEASIBILITY/FEE STUDY

  On September 6, 2023, the City Council adopted an Inclusionary Housing
  Ordinance ("IHO”) and an in-lieu fee formula to encourage affordable housing in
  Monterey Park. The Council also directed the City Manager to assess the IHO’s
  financial feasibility and recommend in-lieu fees where necessary. To assist in this
  evaluation, the City partnered with the San Gabriel Valley Council of Governments
  (“SGVCOG”) and engaged Economic & Planning Systems (“EPS”) for a tailored
  feasibility study.

  On January 17, 2024, the feasibility study was presented to City Council and found
  that the IHO's requirements could present financial challenges for new residential
  projects, particularly smaller and mid-sized developments. Based on this analysis,
  the City Council directed staff to pause enforcement of the IHO for one year and
  revisit its financial feasibility in the coming year.

  EPS was hired to review the previously prepared feasibility study and update it to
  reflect current market conditions. In updating the feasibility study, during the
  Council-directed IHO enforcement pause, EPS looked at both direct and indirect
  factors that may change the financial feasibility of implementing the IHO. The
  study’s overall conclusion states that while the requirements of the IHO are likely
  to remain financially challenging for new residential development within the City
  and may constrain new projects, current market conditions have demonstrated
  improved feasibility of new residential projects overall since the previous analysis.

  Discussion: Director of Community Development Serrano and Planning Manager
  Chow introduced Senior Associate Chinmay Damle and Principal Julie Cooper
  from Economic and Planning Systems Inc. (EPS) to present the City’s feasibility
  study.

  Senior Associate Damle and Principal Cooper from EPS presented a PowerPoint
  Presentation about the City’s Inclusionary Housing Ordinance (IHO) feasibility
  study and provided potential options of consideration to the City Council.

  Action Taken: The City Council received and filed the report and presentation and
  provided direction to staff to as follows: temporarily pause the IHO requirements
  for at least 9 months - 12 months and return to City Council with an updated
  financial feasibility study for consideration by the Council in December or January
  (2026). During this pause, Staff is directed to (1) adjust the requirements of IHO
  relating to projects automatically qualifying for the State Density Bonus and (2) the
  adoption of an in-lieu fee at a level that is higher or equivalent of providing units
  on-site.

3-D.  CONSIDERATION AND POSSIBLE ACTION TO WAIVE SECOND READING OF
  AN ORDINANCE AMENDING THE MONTEREY PARK MUNICIPAL CODE
  CHAPTER 2.32 UPDATING EMPLOYEE RELATIONS

  The City conducted a review of the Employee Relations section in the Monterey
  Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”). This occurred after the California Public
  Employment Relations Board (“PERB”) found that the City’s procedures for
  recognizing associations/unions were insufficient for making an appropriate union
  designation. The proposed changes to MPMC Chapter 2.32 provide the
  appropriate procedures and processes to recognize or appeal new
  associations/unions. City representatives discussed and reviewed the MPMC
  section modification with representatives from the current recognized
  associations/unions. The association/union representatives had an opportunity to
  meet and discuss the impacts of the revisions and the groups agreed with the
  revisions. The proposed amendments to the MPMC provide processes and
  procedures for associations recognition along with appeal and decertification
  procedures.

  The Ordinance was introduced and first reading was waived at the December 18,
  2024 City Council meeting. Second reading and adoption of the Ordinance is
  recommended. If adopted, the ordinance will take effect in 30 days.

  No. 2260 amending Chapter 2.32 of Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”)
  revising Employee Relations procedures, on Consent Calendar.

  escheated to the City in accordance with this AP&P.

  for two (2) successive weeks in a newspaper of general circulation which lists unclaimed
  monies held by the City for more than three (3) years.

  C.  Persons seeking to claim the monies may present satisfactory evidence to the City Treasurer
  regarding their right to recover money. The City Treasurer may then release such monies to
  the depositor, heir, beneficiary, or duly appointed representative at any time before the noticed
  meeting at which the City Council will consider escheating the monies to the general fund
  (Government Code § 50052.5).

  of the City of Monterey Park forty-five (45) days after the initial public notice Pursuant to
  Government Code§§ 50050 and 50051.

  E.  The City Council may transfer unclaimed monies to the General Fund by resolution in
  accordance with Government Code§ 50053.

  F.  Pursuant to Government Code§ 50055, unclaimed monies less than $15.00, or any amount if
  the depositor's name is unknown, which remain unclaimed for the period of one year may be
  transferred to the general fund by the City Council without the necessity of public notification
  in a newspaper.

BACKGROUND:

65302, addressing land use, circulation, housing, noise, safety, conservation and open

The following sections provide an update of the status and implementation of each

Urban Design and Land Use Element
A comprehensive update to the Urban Design and Land Use Element (“LUE”) was
adopted in 2019 and approved by voters in November 2020. Since this time, the City has
processed a variety of new land use developments and adopted new land use regulations
that have continually upheld the LUE.

The following ordinances related to land uses were initiated and adopted in 2024:
  • Aligning residential density standards consistent with the General Plan;
  • Modifying parking requirements related to multi-family housing developments;
  • Modifying emergency shelters regulations consistent with state law;
  • Modifying supportive housing regulations consistent with state law; and
  • Creating standards for data centers.

Addressing the inconsistencies between the LUE and the Monterey Park Municipal Code
(“MPMC”), which implements the LUE, is ongoing. In fall of 2023, the Community
Development Department launched the Our City, Our Plan campaign to make changes
to zoning and update the MPMC with the intention revitalization of the downtown,
expanding housing opportunities and streamlining development. Two sets of zone
changes were approved in early and late 2024 addressing the consistency between the
LUE and MPMC. The City continues to implement the Our City, Our Plan effort.

Economic Development Element
The Economic Development Element, last updated in 2001, helps guide City efforts to
maintain an economically viable range of housing and employment opportunities that
meet the needs of residents and workers. In August of 2024, City Council approved the
Economic Development Strategic Plan.

Last year, the City progressed in helping local small businesses in the following areas:
  • Launching the Monterey Park Business Alliance to support business owners in the
  City of Monterey Park;
  • Hosting a small business expo to provide business owners with resources and an
  opportunity to network;
  • Hosting roundtable meetings with developers and property owners to create
  connections and provide information on opportunities; and
  • Providing monthly e-newsletters with information on training, grants and other
  resources to the City’s business community.

Through the efforts listed above and others in recent years, the City was awarded the
2024 Most Business-Friendly City Award by the Los Angeles County Economic
Development Corporation. This award recognizes the City’s outstanding efforts in
creating a supportive and thriving business environment. The City’s dedication to

Circulation Element
The purpose of the Circulation Element, last updated in 2001, is to define a safe, efficient,
and adequate circulation system in the City. The element also focuses on identification
and evaluation of local circulation needs, while balancing those needs with regional
circulation, public transportation, and bicycle and pedestrian circulation in the Monterey
Park community.

The City has continued to make a variety of street and traffic improvements to its existing
network of public streets and sidewalks including street resurfacing, sidewalk repair,
Americans with Disabilities Act (“ADA”) compliance, installation of bike lanes, and traffic
signal modifications.

These street and traffic improvements are identified as Capital Improvement Projects
(“CIPs”) in which federal, state and local funding sources are utilized to execute the
projects. Some of the projects completed in 2024 include 7.8 miles of resurfaced streets
and 4.5 miles of slurry sealed streets in several residential neighborhoods. The Monterey
Pass Road Rehabilitation occurred in 2024, with a majority of the construction complete
and awaiting final closeout in 2025. Additional improvements to the circulation system
related to traffic signals and sidewalk repairs occurred at key intersections.

Related to transit services, the City completed its evaluation of the Spirit Bus fixed-route
transportation program and is considering changes. These changes may include
adjusting routes and introducing on-demand trip planning, allowing riders to book trips as
needed instead of following fixed routes or schedules like traditional shuttle services. On-
demand systems modernize transit services by incorporating new technology trends,
offering flexible and efficient solutions that respond to the evolving needs of the
community. Decisions related to any changes will be reviewed by Staff and Council in the
future.

Management System (“NIMS”). Trainings have also engaged the community through the

Resources Element
The Resources Element, last updated in 2001, addresses open space and conservation.
Because Monterey Park is a built-out urban community, there are few “natural” resources
such as forests or wildlife habitat or agricultural land. The Resources Element, therefore,
directs policy toward preserving those resources important in the urban environment of
Monterey Park and critical to preserving this City’s heritage for future generations. These
resources include City parks and other improved open space areas, historic resources,
water resources, and air quality.

To further the goals within the Resources Element, the Director has diligently worked to
preserve, enhance, and upgrade open space areas such as the updates and upgrades
to playground equipment throughout the City. Maintenance and upgrade of the City’s
open space facilities are an on-going extension of CIP’s that the City carries out. The
following improvements were completed in 2024 to various City parks and facilities:
  • Sequoia Park – new playground installation;
  • Bella Vista Park – new playground installation;
  • Highlands Park - new playground installation;
  • Garvey Ranch Park - new playground installation; and
  • Edison Trails Park – new playground installation.

Other efforts to implement the Resources Element included the launch of the City’s first
Parks System Master Plan to help shape the future of the City’s open space network and
recreation services. Efforts such as surveys, open house events, and other engagement
activities were employed to help garner community input.

  EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
  After dissolving redevelopment agencies, the California Legislature adopted
  “Economic Opportunity” legislation in 2014, which allows use of public funds to promote
  economic development (SB 470, Wright 2013). Depending on the type of economic
  development a city is seeking to promote, a city may be required to make findings to
  demonstrate that the use of public funds towards economic development initiatives will
  likely create jobs, improve tax revenues, or satisfy a need for affordable housing.

  The City Council’s 2024-2025 Strategic Plan includes a goal to “Strengthen our local
  economy and enhance housing opportunities”. Using elements of the Economic
  Opportunity legislation may help advance this goal.

  The SBAP presents a valuable opportunity to leverage CDBG funding to directly
  support the local business community. By providing targeted financial assistance, the
  program can contribute to the economic recovery, growth, and long-term prosperity of
  Monterey Park.

  Staff requests that the City Council approve the implementation of the SBAP, adopt a
  resolution establishing the program’s policies and procedures as described in

  of the SBAP.

  BACKGROUND:
  Government Code §§ 52200 to 52203 generally allows cities to expend public monies
  to help private enterprises for “economic opportunity.” Under this legislation, a city may
  also issue an economic development subsidy, such as a bond, loan, or incentive. Doing
  so requires a city to comply with certain notice and hearing requirements before
  granting an “economic development subsidy” in the amount of $100,000 or more and
  must provide a report showing the efficacy of the subsidy.

  An “economic development subsidy” is defined as:

  “any expenditure of public funds or loss of revenue to a
  local agency in the amount of one hundred thousand
  dollars ($100,000) or more, for the purpose of stimulating
  economic development within the jurisdiction of a local
  agency including, without limitation, bonds, grants, loans,
  loan guarantees, enterprise zone or empowerment zone
  incentives, fee waivers, land price subsidies, matching
  funds, tax abatements, tax exemptions, and tax credits.”

  Before approving an economic development subsidy, a city must provide certain
  information in a publicly available written form and on the city website. That information
  must remain available during the term of the subsidy. That information includes
  identifying information pertaining to entities (aside from sole proprietorships) receiving

  Within the term of the grant subsidy, but not later than five years following the grant of

SECTION 1: The City Council finds as follows:

  A. Clarissa (Clara) Harlowe Barton is one of the most honored women in American
  history known for her astounding devotion and dedication to helping others. Barton
  is considered a visionary whose humanitarian spirit helped change the world, and
  on May 21, 1881, founded the American Red Cross.

  B. After hearing of the Swiss-inspired global Red Cross network while visiting Europe
  following the Civil War, Barton and a few of her acquaintances campaigned for an
  American Red Cross and ratification of the Geneva Convention protecting the war-
  injured, which the United States ratified in 1882.

  C. Barton led the American Red Cross for 23 years and conducted its very first
  domestic and overseas disaster relief efforts. The American Red Cross also aided
  the U.S. military during the Spanish-American War and successfully campaigned
  for the inclusion of peacetime relief work as part of the global Red Cross network.

  D. The American Red Cross introduced its first aid, water safety, and public health
  nursing program prior to World War I, and by 1918, local chapters grew from 107
  to 3,864 with more than 30 million adult and junior Red Cross members. Following
  the war, the Red Cross focused its service to veterans and enhanced its programs
  in safety training, accident prevention, in-home care, and nutrition education.

  E. Extensive services provided by the American Red Cross were once again needed
  for the U.S. military in World War II. This request initiated a national blood program
  that collected 13.3 million pints of blood for use by the armed forces. Following
  World War II, the Red Cross introduced the first nationwide civilian blood program
  that now supplies more than 40% of the blood and blood products in the United
  States today.

  F. The American Red Cross has since expanded its services to include civil defense,
  CPR/AED training, HIV/AIDS education, and the provision of emotional care and
  support in the wake of disasters and continues to assist government agencies and
  community organizations plan, coordinate and provide feeding, sheltering, and
  family reunification services for people affected by disasters.

  G. Today, the American Red Cross provides compassionate care in five critical areas:
  people affected by disasters in America; support for members of the military and
  their families; blood collection, processing, and distribution; health and safety
  education and training; and international relief and development.

  lifesaving blood, providing education and training, and alleviating human suffering
  in the face of emergencies by mobilizing the power of volunteers and the
  generosity of donors.

  I. The Monterey Park City Council recognizes the compassion of people in the

  A. In February 1980, President Jimmy Carter issued a presidential proclamation
  declaring the week of March 8 as National Women’s History Week. The
  proclamation stated, “From the first settlers who came to our shores, from the first
  American Indian families who befriended them, men and women have worked
  together to build this nation. Too often the women were unsung and sometimes
  their contributions went unnoticed. However, the achievements, leadership,
  courage, strength, and love of the women who built America were as vital as that
  of the men whose names we know so well.”

  B. Women’s History Month originated as a national celebration in 1981 when
  Congress passed Public Law 97-28 which authorized the President to proclaim the
  week beginning March 7, 1982, as Women’s History Week. Throughout the next
  five years, Congress continued to pass joint resolutions designating a week in
  March as Women’s History Week.

  C. In 1987, after being petitioned by the National Women’s History Project, Congress
  passed Public Law 100-9 which designed the month of March 1987 as Women’s
  History Month.

  D. Between 1988 and 1994, Congress passed additional resolutions requesting and
  authorizing the President to proclaim March of each year as Women’s History
  Month. Since 1995, U.S. Presidents, regardless of political party, have issued a
  series of annual proclamations designating the month of March as Women’s
  History Month. These proclamations celebrate the contributions women have
  made and recognize the specific achievements women have made throughout
  American history in a variety of fields.

  E. Women’s History Month corresponds with International Women’s Day which is
  celebrated on March 8 worldwide. It provides an opportunity to celebrate the
  achievements of women while calling for greater equality.

  F. The National Women’s History Alliance designates a yearly theme for Women’s
  History Month. For 2025, the National Women’s History Alliance (NWHA) proudly
  presents the theme “Moving Forward Together! Women Educating & Inspiring

  On December 18, 2024, City Council adopted Resolution No. 2024-R98
  authorizing the City Manager to take necessary measures for the emergency
  replacement of self-contained breathing apparatus for the Fire Department. SCBAs
  are critical personal protective equipment for fire suppression staff, and the Fire
  Department’s current inventory is no longer supported for repairs and replacement
  parts as of December 16, 2024. To ensure fire suppression staff are properly
  protected, the current inventory of SCBAs needs immediate replacement.

  The Fire Chief (“Chief”) obtained a quote from Bauer Compressors, Inc. for the
  replacement of SCBAs, which includes both the items and a comprehensive
  service warranty for $633,812.92.

  The City ordered the replacement SCBAs from Bauer Compressors on December
  19, 2024. The Department received the first shipment of SCBAs the second week
  of January 2025, which contained about 30% of the needed SCBAs and parts.
  Bauer confirmed that the remainder of the order is slated to ship out the second
  week of March. Once the full order has been received, the necessary training and
  calibration will take place before the SCBA’s are deployed for use.

  Action Taken: The City Council received and filed this staff report summarizing
  the status of the emergency replacement of self-contained breathing apparatus on
  Consent Calendar.

  After dissolving redevelopment agencies, the California Legislature adopted
  “Economic Opportunity” legislation in 2014, which allows use of public funds to
  promote economic development (SB 470, Wright 2013). Depending on the type of
  economic development a city is seeking to promote, a city may be required to make
  findings to demonstrate that the use of public funds towards economic
  development initiatives will likely create jobs, improve tax revenues, or satisfy a
  need for affordable housing.

  The City Council’s 2024-2025 Strategic Plan includes a goal to “Strengthen our
  local economy and enhance housing opportunities”. Using elements of the
  Economic Opportunity legislation may help advance this goal.

  The SBAP presents a valuable opportunity to leverage CDBG funding to directly
  support the local business community. By providing targeted financial assistance,
  the program can contribute to the economic recovery, growth, and long-term
  prosperity of Monterey Park.

  where there is possibility that it may have a significant effect on the environment,
  activities that do not constitute a “project” as defined, and actions to protect the
  environment, respectively. This activity is for general policies and procedure-
  making intended to promote economic development. Any subsequent construction
